summary: Defines S/MIME version 4.0, a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Digital signatures give authentication, integrity, and proof of origin, encryption gives confidentiality, and compression can reduce size. It obsoletes RFC 5751 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: S/MIME defines formats for signing, encrypting, and compressing MIME content. Its message formats let receiving software check signatures or decrypt content using the algorithms the specification requires.

subtitle: Specifies MIME message formats and algorithms for signing, encrypting, and compressing content.

tldr.problem: MIME messages need interoperable formats for applying cryptographic signatures, encryption, and compression. Earlier S/MIME algorithms and requirements also needed an update.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME prepares a canonical MIME entity and wraps it in a Cryptographic Message Syntax object. It defines signed, enveloped, authenticated-enveloped, and compressed message forms.
tldr.outcome: Version 4.0 adds AuthEnvelopedData and updates supported algorithms. It obsoletes RFC 5751 and has been updated by RFC 9788.

today: RFC 8551 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2019 and obsoletes RFC 5751. It has been updated by RFC 9788.

sections.title: What S/MIME Provides
sections.content:
Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) defines a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Digital signatures provide authentication, message integrity, and proof of origin; encryption provides confidentiality; compression can reduce message size.

S/MIME can carry MIME data over transports other than email, including HTTP or SIP. RFC 8551 defines how cryptographic services use Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) objects and MIME media types.
sections.plainLanguage: S/MIME adds signatures, encryption, or compression to MIME content. It can be used wherever a transport carries MIME data, not only in email.

sections.title: Required Algorithms and CMS Types
sections.content:
Version 4.0 requires support for SHA-256 and SHA-512 digests. For signatures, receiving agents must support ECDSA with P-256 and SHA-256, and EdDSA with curve25519 in PureEdDSA mode; sending agents must support at least one of those two algorithms.

Agents must support AES-128 GCM and AES-256 GCM for content encryption. The specification also defines support levels for other algorithms, including AES-128 CBC and ChaCha20-Poly1305. The CMS content types used by S/MIME include SignedData, EnvelopedData, AuthEnvelopedData, and CompressedData.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets common algorithm requirements so different S/MIME agents can exchange messages. It requires support for two digest algorithms and two authenticated-encryption algorithms.

sections.title: Preparing MIME Content
sections.content:
Before signing, enveloping, or compressing, the sender prepares a canonical MIME entity. The process prepares the entity, converts its leaf parts to canonical form, and applies suitable transfer encoding.

Text MIME entities must use carriage-return and line-feed pairs as line endings, and their character sets must be canonicalized. A sender may wrap a full message in message/rfc822 when it wants to protect outer headers such as Subject, To, From, and Cc.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides need the same representation of the MIME content before cryptographic checks can work. Text line endings must use the specified two-character form.

sections.title: Signed, Enveloped, and Compressed Messages
sections.content:
An EnvelopedData message encrypts content but does not provide integrity by itself. AuthEnvelopedData provides confidentiality and integrity, but not proof of who sent the message. SignedData carries a signature inside a CMS object.

A clear-signed message uses multipart/signed: its first part contains readable content and its second part carries a detached application/pkcs7-signature. CompressedData reduces message size but does not provide security services. These forms can be nested, and receiving agents must process nested S/MIME within reasonable resource limits.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing, encryption, and compression provide different services. A readable clear-signed message keeps its content visible and carries the signature as a separate part.

sections.title: Certificates and Key Sizes
sections.content:
Receiving agents must provide a way to retrieve recipient certificates. This RFC describes what agents do after a certificate has been validated or rejected; certificate handling itself is covered elsewhere.

Key pairs must use a good source of non-deterministic random input, and private keys must be protected. An S/MIME user agent must not generate RSA signature keys smaller than 2048 bits. The RFC gives separate requirements for generating and verifying signatures with RSA keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Agents need certificates to verify signatures and encrypt messages for recipients. Keys must be generated with suitable randomness, and private keys must be protected.

sections.title: Security Limits and Message Handling
sections.content:
Unauthenticated EnvelopedData can be modified without detection, which is one reason the RFC adds authenticated encryption. Authenticated encryption alone does not prove which person sent a message; the key and message structure must meet additional conditions, and the sender cannot prove origin to a third party using a key shared with the recipient.

Sending the same content with weaker encryption can expose content protected by stronger encryption. The RFC also warns that message lengths can reveal information and that compression with encryption must avoid creating a compression oracle. Mail clients must finish integrity checks before acting on decrypted content.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption can hide content without proving who sent it. A sender should not also send a weaker encrypted copy that could reveal the same content.
